info.about: The most photographed wave on earth and the most consequential. Pipeline breaks over a shallow, cavernous lava reef only a few hundred metres off Ehukai Beach Park, throwing a thick left-hand barrel that ends in dry rock. Backdoor peels right off the same peak. When the North Pacific lights up between November and February the whole surfing world points its cameras here.
info.wave: Heaving left barrel; Backdoor is the right
info.bestWind: Light E/NE trades or glassy dawn
info.crowd: Extreme in season — a strict pecking order
info.localTip: Watch a full set from the beach before paddling. If you are asking whether you are ready, you are not.

access.transfer: About 60 min by car from Honolulu up the H-2 and Kam Highway
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: The birthplace of modern big-wave surfing. Waimea sleeps flat most of the year, then wakes up when the North Pacific sends 20-foot-plus swell, producing a giant right-hand peak that breaks into a deepwater bay. The Eddie Aikau invitational runs here only when the bay says it can.
info.wave: Steep, fast drop into a bowling right
info.crowd: Small but elite lineup; huge shorebreak crowd on the sand
hazards: Strong rip out of the bay
Only ride it if you can swim it
info.localTip: The rip along the rocks on the north side is the standard paddle-out lane on big days.

access.transfer: About 55 min drive from Honolulu
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: A huge, shifting right-hand peak over a wide reef, and the North Shore's most demanding paddle. Sunset rewards positioning over speed: the takeoff zone moves with every set and the West Bowl can turn a good wave into a great one. It has been a contest venue since the sport professionalised.
info.wave: Big, shifting right with a bowling inside section
info.crowd: Busy but spread out over a big playing field
info.localTip: Line up off the point and be ready to scratch wide; the second wave of a set is usually the better one.

access.transfer: About 60 min drive from Honolulu
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: Where surfing was reintroduced to the world. Waikiki's outer reefs produce slow, forgiving rollers that can run for 200 metres or more, perfect for longboards and first waves. Duke Kahanamoku's statue faces the break he made famous, and the beachboy tradition of teaching visitors here is over a century old.
info.bestTide: Mid to high tide is safest over the reef
info.crowd: Very busy but friendly and forgiving
info.localTip: Queens is the pick of the peaks; go at dawn before the catamarans and lessons arrive.

access.transfer: 15 min from Honolulu airport
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: Maui's north-shore proving ground and the world capital of windsurfing. Ho'okipa has three reef peaks — Pavilions, Middles and Lanes — that handle serious size, and a cliff-top car park that makes it one of the best waves on earth to simply watch. Green sea turtles haul out on the beach most afternoons.
info.wave: Punchy rights and lefts across three peaks
info.bestWind: Light SW or early morning glass
info.crowd: Crowded; surfers have the morning, windsurfers take over after about 11am
hazards: Trade winds get violent by midday
info.localTip: Surf it before 11am. Local etiquette hands the water over to the sailors when the wind fills in.

access.transfer: About 20 min east of Kahului on the Hana Highway
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: Surf City USA. A long stretch of consistent beach break either side of a concrete pier, with peaks that suit everyone from first-timers to the pros who show up for the US Open every summer. It is rarely world class and almost never flat, which is exactly why the whole industry grew up around it.
info.bestSwell: SW summer swell or NW winter swell
info.crowd: Very crowded, especially south of the pier
info.localTip: The sandbars either side of the pier shift constantly — walk the beach and pick your peak rather than paddling out where everyone else is.

access.transfer: 20 min from John Wayne (SNA); about 50 min from LAX
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: The most influential right-hand point in surfing. On a good south swell Malibu links three points into a single, tapering wall that can run the length of the beach — the wave that shaped longboarding, then shortboarding, then the entire California myth. It is also a designated World Surfing Reserve.
info.level: Intermediate; crowded enough to demand skill
info.crowd: Extreme — one of the most crowded waves in the world
info.localTip: Third Point is where the wave starts; ride it through and you get the whole thing. Weekday dawn is the only quiet window.

access.transfer: About 45 min up the Pacific Coast Highway from LAX
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: A cliff-side right-hand point in the heart of Santa Cruz, with four distinct peaks and a natural amphitheatre of onlookers along West Cliff Drive. The Lane handles size, holds shape in wind that ruins everywhere else, and has been the proving ground for Northern Californian surfing since the 1930s.
info.wave: Powerful right with a steep drop; Middle Peak holds size
info.waterTemp: 11–15°C — 4/3 wetsuit and boots on cold days
info.crowd: Crowded and territorial
hazards: Great white sharks are present in the region
info.localTip: Watch from the lighthouse for twenty minutes first; each of the four peaks wants a different lineup.

access.transfer: About 45 min over the hill from San Jose
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: Three miles of raw, cold, unforgiving beach break at the edge of San Francisco. The paddle out is legendary — multiple lines of whitewater, ferocious rips and water that rarely climbs out of the low teens. When it is good it is as heavy as any beach break in the world.
info.wave: Thick, close-out prone A-frames; big and fast when it works
info.waterTemp: 11–14°C — 4/3 with hood and boots in winter
info.crowd: Uncrowded, because it is hard
info.localTip: Use the rip to get out, never to come in. Sloat and Noriega break differently — check both.

access.transfer: 25 min across the city from SFO
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: San Diego's coast runs from mellow Pacific Beach peaks to Blacks Beach, where the Scripps submarine canyon funnels swell into some of the most powerful beach break in California. Sun, consistency and a hundred kilometres of coastline make it the easiest place in the US to surf every day.
info.breakType: Beach break over a submarine canyon
info.wave: Powerful, wedging peaks at Blacks; softer at PB
info.bestSwell: W–NW winter or S summer swell
info.crowd: Busy but spread across many beaches
hazards: Long, steep trail down to Blacks
info.localTip: Blacks doubles in size relative to the rest of the coast — check the buoy, not the neighbouring beach.

access.transfer: 20–30 min from San Diego airport
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: Kelly Slater's home beach and the friendliest place in the US to learn. The Atlantic here delivers small, soft, warm-water peaks most of the year, going properly good when a hurricane swell or a winter nor'easter arrives. The pier is the landmark and the meeting point.
info.bestSwell: E–NE swell; hurricane season brings the size
info.bestSeason: August–November for size; year round for learning
info.crowd: Busy near the pier, empty a mile either way
info.localTip: When the forecast is flat here it usually is. Watch the tropics — a distant hurricane transforms this coast.

access.transfer: About 60 min east from Orlando; 20 min from Melbourne
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: The best wave in Florida and the training ground of a generation of American professionals. The north jetty focuses swell into a fast, rampy right-hander — 'First Peak' — that is the closest thing the east coast has to a performance wave, and the contest site that produced Slater, Lopez and the Hobgoods.
info.wave: Fast, wedging right with an air section
info.crowd: Very crowded at First Peak; spread out down the beach
hazards: Sharks are common around the inlet
info.localTip: If First Peak is a zoo, walk south — the beach picks up the same swell with a tenth of the crowd.

access.transfer: About 40 min south of Melbourne, FL
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: A 200-mile sandbar hanging off the American east coast, and the best beach break on it. When a hurricane tracks offshore in September the OBX sandbars produce genuinely world-class barrels; the rest of the year it is windswept, empty and wildly variable.
info.bestSwell: E–SE hurricane swell or winter NE
info.crowd: Empty outside hurricane season
info.localTip: Rent a car and drive: the sandbars change every storm and the best peak is rarely at the same milepost twice.

access.transfer: About 90 min south from Norfolk, Virginia
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: A long, sandy municipal beach with a pier at First Street that focuses whatever swell the mid-Atlantic offers. It is not a world-class wave but it is consistent, easy to access, and home to the East Coast Surfing Championships — the oldest continuously running surf contest in the world.
info.wave: Short, punchy peaks near the pier
info.bestSwell: NE winter swell or SE hurricane swell
info.crowd: Busy at the pier in summer
info.localTip: The peaks right on the pier pilings are best but are usually closed to surfing in peak summer — check local flags.

access.transfer: 25 min from Norfolk airport
access.visaNote: US ESTA/visa required for most non-US visitors

info.about: The Mexican Pipeline: the heaviest beach break on the planet. A deep offshore trench lets long-period South Pacific swell march straight into the sand at Zicatela, unloading in giant, square barrels that regularly top 20 feet. It is a big-wave venue that happens to break on a beach.
info.crowd: Small crew of specialists; heavy respect required
hazards: Vicious rips and a brutal shorebreak
info.localTip: La Punta at the south end is the friendly wave; Zicatela is not. Know the difference before you paddle.

access.transfer: 10 min from Puerto Escondido airport; about 2.5h from Huatulco
access.visaNote: Most nationalities get a visa on arrival for Mexico

info.about: A cobblestone town on Banderas Bay that turned a gentle right-hand point into a whole surf-school economy. The wave is soft, warm and forgiving, the town is full of taco stands and hammocks, and the harder waves at Punta Mita and Burros are twenty minutes up the road.
info.wave: Slow, mellow rights and a shorter left
info.crowd: Very busy with schools; go early
info.localTip: Paddle 20 minutes north to Carricitos or drive to La Lancha for the same swell without the school crowd.

access.transfer: About 50 min north from Puerto Vallarta
access.visaNote: Most nationalities get a visa on arrival for Mexico

info.about: Guanacaste's surf hub: a wide, sandy bay with a rivermouth sandbar, warm water year round and an easy inside section that has taught thousands of people to surf. Witch's Rock and Ollie's Point are a boat ride north, which is why so many trips base themselves here.
info.breakType: Beach break with a rivermouth bank
info.wave: Long, soft rights on the rivermouth; peaky beach break inside
info.bestWind: E offshore in the dry season
info.bestSeason: April–October for swell; December–April for offshore wind
info.crowd: Busy but the bay is wide enough
hazards: Crocodiles in the estuary — do not cross the rivermouth
Strong rip on the north side
info.localTip: Book a panga to Witch's Rock for a dawn session; it is one of the great day trips in surfing.

access.transfer: About 75 min from Liberia; roughly 5h from San José
access.visaNote: Most nationalities get 90 days visa-free in Costa Rica

info.about: A dirt-road beach town on the tip of the Nicoya Peninsula with kilometres of consistent, punchy beach break and some of the most reliable offshore mornings in Central America. It went from fishing village to international surf destination in about fifteen years and the swell has never noticed.
info.wave: Punchy A-frames, hollow at low tide
info.bestTide: Mid tide rising; low is hollow
info.crowd: Spread along a long beach — easy to find space
info.localTip: The bank in front of Playa Carmen is the most consistent; walk north toward Playa Hermosa for cleaner peaks.

access.transfer: About 5h by road plus ferry from San José, or a 40-min light aircraft hop to Tambor
access.visaNote: Most nationalities get 90 days visa-free in Costa Rica

info.about: Chile's most famous wave: a long, powerful left-hand point that peels past two sea stacks below dramatic cliffs. It handles huge swell, has hosted big-wave events, and is protected as a World Surfing Reserve after a local campaign saved the headland from development.
info.bestSeason: April–September for size; year round consistency
info.crowd: Moderate; the wave is long enough to share
hazards: Very strong current on big days
info.localTip: The jump-off from the rocks is the standard entry; time it with the sets rather than fighting the paddle from the beach.

access.transfer: About 3.5h south-west by road from Santiago
access.visaNote: Many nationalities enter Chile visa-free for 90 days

info.about: An island with more than forty beaches and a wave for every wind. Joaquina is the contest beach and the birthplace of Brazilian competitive surfing; Praia Mole, Campeche and Silveira spread the crowd across the island. Brazil's surf industry effectively lives here.
info.bestWind: N–NW offshore for the east-coast beaches
info.crowd: Busy in summer; quiet mid-week in winter
hazards: Urban water quality in some bays
info.localTip: With this many beaches, let the wind pick the spot — there is almost always somewhere offshore on the island.

access.transfer: 20–40 min by car depending on which beach
access.visaNote: Check Brazil's current visa rules for your nationality

info.about: Surfing under the Christ statue. Arpoador, the rock between Ipanema and Copacabana, is the city's best-known peak — a short, punchy right with a sunset ritual and a permanent crowd. Barra and Recreio down the coast take more swell and give more room.
info.crowd: Arpoador is packed; Recreio is not
hazards: Petty theft on the beach — take nothing
info.localTip: Arpoador at sunrise is the session; the rock gets a round of applause at sunset for a reason.

access.transfer: About 45 min from Galeão to the south-zone beaches
access.visaNote: Check Brazil's current visa rules for your nationality

info.about: The biggest rideable waves ever surfed. An underwater canyon 5km deep funnels North Atlantic swell straight into the headland at Praia do Norte, focusing it into peaks that have exceeded 25 metres. Most people come to watch from the lighthouse fort — which is the right call.
info.bestSwell: Huge NW Atlantic groundswell with long period
info.crowd: Tiny water crew; enormous crowd on the cliff
hazards: Lethal for anyone but professionals with ski support
info.localTip: Watch from Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo. For actually surfing, Praia do Sul in town is the sane option.

access.transfer: About 90 min north of Lisbon by motorway
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

externalCams.title: MEO Beachcam — Praia do Norte, the canyon
MEO Beachcam — Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo

info.about: Europe's only World Surfing Reserve: seven world-class reefs inside four kilometres of coast. Ribeira d'Ilhas is the long, rippable right that hosts contests; Coxos is the heavy one the locals guard; Pedra Branca is the barrel. A fishing town that became the best-value surf trip in Europe.
info.wave: Long walling rights at Ribeira; hollow and heavy at Coxos
info.level: Intermediate to expert depending on the reef
info.crowd: Busy at Ribeira, guarded at Coxos
info.localTip: Start at Ribeira d'Ilhas. Earn Coxos later, and only when it is not crowded with locals.

access.transfer: About 50 min north-west of Lisbon
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The European Pipeline. Supertubos is a sand-bottom beach break that throws thick, fast, perfectly round barrels when a NW swell meets the right bank — heavy enough to hold a championship-tour event. Peniche's peninsula also means there is a beach facing every wind direction.
info.crowd: Crowded when it is on
info.localTip: If Supertubos is closing out, drive ten minutes to Baleal — the peninsula almost always has a sheltered option.

access.transfer: About 75 min north of Lisbon
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: Lisbon's home beach: 15 kilometres of sand break starting a bridge-crossing from the city centre. A series of groynes creates dozens of banks, so there is nearly always a peak with space, and the whole coast is reachable on public transport from the capital.
info.crowd: Busy near the town, empty further south
hazards: Occasional water quality issues after storms
info.localTip: Take the beach train south in summer — the further you go, the emptier and cleaner the banks.

access.transfer: About 30 min from Lisbon across the 25 de Abril bridge
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The best left-hand rivermouth in Europe, and possibly the world. When a big NW swell meets the sandbar at the mouth of the Urdaibai estuary, Mundaka produces a long, hollow, spinning left that can run for 400 metres. It is fickle, tide-dependent and worth the wait.
info.bestTide: Mid-to-low outgoing tide is the classic window
info.crowd: Very crowded and strictly hierarchical when it is on
hazards: Strong local pecking order — wait your turn
info.localTip: The jetty jump-off saves a brutal paddle. If it is firing, expect a full lineup of very good local surfers.

access.transfer: About 45 min east from Bilbao
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The Basque country's longest beach and its most consistent, a 2.5km arc that picks up almost any swell and has been hosting European contests for decades. The town behind it is a pintxos crawl, which makes it an unusually civilised place to base a surf trip.
info.crowd: Busy in town, quieter at either end
hazards: Water can be choppy in onshore winds
info.localTip: The west end near the campsite has the best banks; the east end is calmer for learning.

access.transfer: About 25 min from San Sebastián; 60 min from Bilbao
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A surf beach in the middle of one of Europe's great food cities. Zurriola sits right in San Sebastián, exposed enough to pick up swell that the sheltered La Concha bay never sees, with a wall of pintxos bars two streets back from the sand.
info.level: Intermediate; beginner areas at the west end
info.crowd: Busy — it is a city beach
info.localTip: Surf at dawn, eat pintxos in the Parte Vieja at night. That is the whole itinerary and it is a good one.

access.transfer: 20 min from Hondarribia (EAS); 90 min from Bilbao
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The best beach break in Europe. The Gouf de Capbreton — a deep submarine canyon running right up to the shore — supercharges Atlantic swell into thick, hollow barrels at La Gravière and the surrounding banks. Europe's surf industry is headquartered here for a reason.
info.breakType: Beach break over a submarine canyon
info.crowd: Crowded in season
hazards: Very heavy waves for a beach break
info.localTip: September is the sweet spot: warm water, big Atlantic swell and offshore mornings. Check the banks daily.

access.transfer: About 35 min north of Biarritz
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: Where European surfing began, in 1957, when a Hollywood screenwriter left a board behind. The Grande Plage sits below belle-époque hotels and a casino; Côte des Basques is the longboard beach at low tide; Marbella and Milady take the swell when it gets big.
info.wave: Mellow longboard walls to punchy beach peaks
info.bestTide: Côte des Basques needs low tide
info.crowd: Busy in summer, pleasant in autumn
hazards: Rocks at low tide on some beaches
info.localTip: Côte des Basques at low tide on a small clean swell is one of the nicest longboard sessions in Europe.

access.transfer: 10 min from Biarritz airport
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A pine-forest beach town north of Bordeaux with a long, consistent stretch of Atlantic beach break and a European contest pedigree. Less heavy than Hossegor, more forgiving, and backed by 100km of cycle paths through the forest.
info.crowd: Busy in July and August only
info.localTip: Ride a bike north from the town centre and pick an empty bank — there are kilometres of them.

access.transfer: About 60 min west from Bordeaux
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The centre of British surfing. Fistral faces straight into Atlantic swell, holds size better than most UK beaches, and has hosted the country's major contests for decades. The Cribbar, the big-wave reef off the headland, only shows up a few days a year.
info.wave: Punchy peaks; holds size at North Fistral
info.crowd: Busy, especially in summer
info.localTip: When Fistral is blown out, cross the peninsula to Watergate Bay or head to the north coast's sheltered coves.

access.transfer: 10 min from Newquay Cornwall airport
access.visaNote: Check UK entry requirements for your nationality

info.about: Ireland's surf capital, on the wild Atlantic coast of Donegal. The Peak is a heavy left and right reef right in front of town, and the surrounding coast hides some of the heaviest slabs in Europe. Cold, raw and consistently good from autumn onwards.
info.wave: Hollow, powerful left and right off a reef
info.waterTemp: 8–15°C — 5/4 with hood, gloves and boots in winter
info.crowd: Small, dedicated crew
info.localTip: Bring the warmest wetsuit you own. The Atlantic here does not care what the calendar says.

access.transfer: About 60 min from Knock; roughly 3h from Dublin
access.visaNote: Ireland is outside Schengen — check entry requirements

info.about: A friendly beach break in a golf-and-surf town on the Clare coast, twenty minutes from the Cliffs of Moher. The beach is forgiving and good for learning; the reefs either side — including the notorious Aileen's under the cliffs — are anything but.
info.wave: Mellow beach peaks; heavy reefs on the flanks
info.level: Beginner on the beach, expert on the reefs
info.bestTide: Mid to high tide on the beach
info.crowd: Relaxed
hazards: Powerful reefs nearby — do not wander onto them
Strong currents at the river end
info.localTip: The beach is a genuinely good place to learn. Aileen's, under the Cliffs of Moher, is not a place to visit casually.

access.transfer: About 60 min from Shannon
access.visaNote: Ireland is outside Schengen — check entry requirements

info.about: The Canaries' windswept desert island, with a north shore full of reefs — Hierro, Bristol, Mejillones, Generosa — that fire on winter Atlantic swell. Warm water, volcanic rock and a lunar landscape; the trade winds that make it a windsurfing capital also ruin the surf if you time it wrong.
info.crowd: Busy on the good reefs in winter
hazards: Very sharp volcanic reef — booties are common
info.localTip: The whole north shore is reef. Get a good pair of booties and study the entry and exit before you paddle out.

access.transfer: About 45 min north from Fuerteventura airport to Corralejo
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A volcanic island where a 6km beach under a 600m cliff (Famara) sits half an hour from El Quemao, the Canaries' most serious barrel. Warm water in winter, consistent Atlantic swell, and a landscape that looks like another planet.
info.bottom: Sand at Famara; lava reef at La Santa
info.wave: Mellow at Famara; heavy barrels at El Quemao
info.level: Beginner at Famara, expert at El Quemao
info.crowd: Famara is busy with schools; the reefs are guarded
hazards: El Quemao is for experts only
info.localTip: Famara for learning and long days; El Quemao only if you genuinely belong there.

access.transfer: About 35 min from Arrecife to Famara
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The south of Tenerife has a run of punchy lava reefs — Las Américas, La Fitenia, Spanish Left — that work on winter NW swell in T-shirt water. It is the most accessible Canarian surf, with an airport, a resort strip and reef breaks in the same square kilometre.
info.bestWind: NE trade winds can be offshore on some reefs
info.crowd: Crowded on the accessible reefs
info.localTip: Booties are worth packing. The reefs are shallow and the rock is volcanic glass in places.

access.transfer: About 20 min from Tenerife South airport
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A former fishing village turned surf town, with a run of long right-hand points down the coast. Anchor Point is the jewel — a 500-metre wall over boulders that works on winter NW swell — and Killer Point, Boilers and Panorama are all within a short drive.
info.crowd: Busy in peak season; the points are long enough to absorb it
info.localTip: The rock jump at Anchor Point is the fast way out. Watch a local do it once before you try.

access.transfer: About 45 min north from Agadir
access.visaNote: Many nationalities enter Morocco visa-free for 90 days

info.about: The most perfect right-hand point on earth. Supertubes runs down a rock ledge in a series of named sections — Boneyards, Supers, Impossibles, Tubes — that on the right day link into a 400-metre high-speed barrel. Championship tour venue, and the standard every other right is measured against.
info.bestTide: All tides; mid is the classic
info.crowd: Very crowded when it is on, with a strict order
info.localTip: Paddle out at Boneyards and let the current do the work. Do not drop in — this lineup polices itself.

access.transfer: About 60 min west from Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth)
access.visaNote: Many nationalities get 90 days visa-free in South Africa

info.about: Cape Town's learn-to-surf beach, with its row of candy-coloured bathing boxes and a long, gentle sandbank that has been teaching people to stand up since the 1910s. Table Mountain is the backdrop and the water is a good deal warmer than the Atlantic side of the peninsula.
info.wave: Long, slow, forgiving rights and lefts
info.bestSwell: S–SW swell wrapping into False Bay
info.crowd: Very busy with schools
hazards: Great white sharks in False Bay — heed the shark spotters' flags
info.localTip: The shark spotters on the mountain fly flags for a reason. Learn the flag system before you paddle out.

access.transfer: About 40 min from Cape Town airport
access.visaNote: Many nationalities get 90 days visa-free in South Africa

info.about: The wave that opened Indonesia to the world in 1971. Uluwatu is a series of left-hand reef sections — Racetrack, Outside Corner, The Peak, Temples — running below a clifftop temple, accessed through a cave that you enter and exit with the tide. On a big dry-season swell it is one of the great waves anywhere.
info.wave: Long, fast, barrelling lefts across several sections
info.bestWind: SE trade winds — offshore in the dry season
info.bestTide: Mid to high; the cave exit needs water
info.crowd: Crowded, but the reef is long
hazards: The cave entry closes out at low tide
Reef cuts infect fast in the tropics
info.localTip: Time your exit with the tide — people get stuck outside the cave every season. Antiseptic for reef cuts is not optional.

access.transfer: About 60 min south from Denpasar
access.visaNote: Visa on arrival for most nationalities in Indonesia

info.about: Bali's most developed surf town: Batu Bolong is a soft, mellow reef-and-sand wave that suits longboards and learners, Echo Beach next door is a punchier reef, and the whole strip is cafés, scooters and sunset crowds. Consistent, warm and endlessly social.
info.wave: Mellow rolling lefts and rights at Batu Bolong; punchier at Echo
info.bestWind: E–SE offshore in the dry season
info.crowd: Very crowded — one of the busiest lineups in Asia
hazards: Rocks and reef at low tide
Water quality in the wet season
info.localTip: Dawn patrol is the only uncrowded window. By 8am Batu Bolong has a hundred people in the water.

access.transfer: About 45 min north-west from Denpasar
access.visaNote: Visa on arrival for most nationalities in Indonesia

info.about: The sandy beach break where most people in Asia catch their first wave. Kuta is a long, forgiving stretch of sand a few minutes from Bali's airport, with soft waves, warm water, board rental every fifty metres and a sunset that draws the whole island.
info.bestWind: E offshore in the dry season
info.crowd: Extremely busy with lessons
info.localTip: Ten minutes from the airport, which makes it the ideal first or last session of a Bali trip.

access.transfer: 10 min from Denpasar airport
access.visaNote: Visa on arrival for most nationalities in Indonesia

info.about: The most famous city beach in the world. A one-kilometre arc of sand in eastern Sydney with a punchy south-end bank (the Backpackers' Express rip runs beside it), a gentler north end, and a permanent cast of swimmers, lifeguards and locals. Not the best wave in Sydney, but the most alive.
info.wave: Short, punchy peaks; better at the south end
info.crowd: Very busy; surfing is restricted to the flagged-free zones
hazards: Strong rips, especially at the south end
Swimming zones limit where you can surf
info.localTip: Bondi is often onshore junk while Maroubra or the northern beaches are clean — check before committing.

access.transfer: About 30 min from Sydney airport
access.visaNote: Australia requires an ETA or visa for almost all visitors

info.about: The longest sand-bottomed right in the world, created by accident. A river-dredging project pumped sand around the point in the 1990s and joined Snapper, Rainbow Bay, Greenmount and Kirra into a single bank that on the right swell can carry a wave nearly two kilometres.
info.level: Advanced — because of the crowd as much as the wave
info.crowd: Among the most crowded lineups on earth
hazards: Extreme crowd — hundreds out on a good day
info.localTip: The takeoff at Snapper Rocks is a queue. If you want waves rather than a fight, sit down the line at Greenmount.

access.transfer: 10 min from Gold Coast airport
access.visaNote: Australia requires an ETA or visa for almost all visitors

info.about: Home of the world's longest-running surf contest, held every Easter since 1962, and the trophy every professional wants to ring. Bells is a big, cold, powerful right-hand point in a natural amphitheatre of cliffs on the Great Ocean Road — a wave that rewards long, drawn-out turns.
info.crowd: Busy in season; the Bowl gets the crowd
hazards: Great whites are present in Victorian waters
info.localTip: Winkipop next door is faster and often better than Bells itself — do not walk past it.

access.transfer: About 35 min from Avalon; roughly 90 min from Melbourne
access.visaNote: Australia requires an ETA or visa for almost all visitors

info.about: Australia's easternmost point, and a long, sand-bottomed right-hand point that is one of the great longboard waves in the country. The Pass runs off Cape Byron in slow, tapering walls under a lighthouse, with dolphins in the lineup most mornings and whales passing through in winter.
info.crowd: Extremely crowded — it is a famous, easy wave
hazards: Sharks have been an issue in the region
info.localTip: Wategos and Little Wategos further round the cape take the same swell with a fraction of the people.

access.transfer: About 30 min from Ballina Byron Gateway
access.visaNote: Australia requires an ETA or visa for almost all visitors

info.about: A big, thick, cold-water reef break that handles serious Indian Ocean swell and hosts a championship tour event. The wider region — from Yallingup to Gracetown — has dozens of reefs, world-class wineries and some of the clearest water in Australia.
info.wave: Thick, powerful right and left off a deep reef
info.crowd: Moderate; the region spreads people out
hazards: Powerful swell that jumps in size fast
Great white sharks — this coast has a genuine record
Remote sections with no help nearby
info.localTip: The swell here can double between checks. Judge it from the car park over a full set cycle, not a single wave.

access.transfer: About 45 min from Busselton; roughly 3h from Perth
access.visaNote: Australia requires an ETA or visa for almost all visitors

info.about: Black volcanic sand, Lion Rock in the middle of the bay, and heavy Tasman Sea beach break forty minutes from central Auckland. Piha is beautiful and genuinely dangerous — it is New Zealand's most rescue-heavy beach and the subject of a long-running documentary series about its lifeguards.
info.crowd: Busy in summer, empty in winter
hazards: Notorious rip currents — swim between the flags
info.localTip: The rips here are the strongest in New Zealand. If you are unsure, surf beside the patrolled flags.

access.transfer: About 45 min west from Auckland
access.visaNote: NZ requires an NZeTA for visa-waiver visitors

info.about: One of the longest left-hand points on the planet, made famous by 'The Endless Summer'. Manu Bay, Whale Bay and Indicators run down a boulder coastline west of Raglan and on a big clean SW swell they link into a ride that can last well over a minute.
info.crowd: Busy but the point is long
info.localTip: Walk further down to Whale Bay if Manu Bay is stacked; it is the same swell with fewer people.

access.transfer: About 45 min from Hamilton; roughly 2h from Auckland
access.visaNote: NZ requires an NZeTA for visa-waiver visitors

info.about: Japanese surf culture's home beach, an hour from central Tokyo. Shonan wraps around Enoshima island with Mount Fuji on the horizon on clear winter days. The waves are usually small and soft — which is why it is packed with everyone from grandmothers on longboards to Olympic-level shortboarders.
info.bestSwell: S–SE swell; typhoon swell is the good stuff
info.crowd: Extremely crowded on weekends
hazards: Typhoon swell arrives fast and big
info.localTip: Weekday mornings are civil; weekends are a scrum. Typhoon season is when Shonan actually gets good.

access.transfer: About 60 min by train from Tokyo to Enoshima
access.visaNote: Japan is visa-free for many nationalities

info.about: The Pacific-facing coast east of Tokyo, and the host of surfing's Olympic debut at Tsurigasaki Beach in 2021. Chiba picks up far more swell than Shonan, with a long run of beach breaks that turn on hard during typhoon season.
info.bestSwell: E–SE swell; typhoon swell in autumn
info.crowd: Busy on weekends with Tokyo crowds
info.localTip: Ichinomiya is the hub, but the coast runs for 60km — drive until you find an empty bank.

access.transfer: About 60 min by car from Narita
access.visaNote: Japan is visa-free for many nationalities

info.about: A long, sandy right-hand point on Sri Lanka's east coast that is one of the friendliest quality point breaks in the world. Warm water, a long peeling wall, elephants in the lagoons behind the town, and a season that runs exactly opposite the island's west coast.
info.crowd: Busy in season but the point is long
hazards: Occasional crocodiles in the nearby lagoons — not the surf
info.localTip: Whiskey Point and Peanut Farm up the coast are quieter versions of the same wave.

access.transfer: About 8h by road across the island from Colombo, or a light-aircraft transfer
access.visaNote: Sri Lanka requires an ETA for most nationalities

info.about: A wide bay on the south coast with a sandy bottom and waist-high waves that break for a very long way — which makes it one of the best value learn-to-surf destinations in the world. Mirissa and the reefs at Midigama are ten minutes away when you want more.
info.wave: Slow, soft, long-running whitewater and small walls
info.crowd: Very busy with schools
hazards: Shallow rocks at the eastern end
info.localTip: When Weligama gets too crowded, Midigama's reefs are a ten-minute tuk-tuk away and far better waves.

access.transfer: About 2.5h south by expressway from Colombo
access.visaNote: Sri Lanka requires an ETA for most nationalities

info.about: The wave that put the Philippines on the surf map: a thick, hollow right-hand reef barrel breaking over shallow coral, with a wooden boardwalk running out to a viewing tower above the lineup. Siargao itself is a teardrop island of palms, lagoons and dirt roads.
info.bestTide: Mid to high tide — low is dangerously shallow
info.crowd: Crowded at the peak; other reefs nearby are quiet
info.localTip: Do not surf Cloud 9 at low tide. Rent a scooter and find the dozen other reefs on the island instead.

access.transfer: 15 min from Siargao airport to General Luna
access.visaNote: Many nationalities get 30 days visa-free in the Philippines

info.about: A genuine urban surf scene on the Mediterranean, where the waves are small, short-period and wind-driven — and the lineup is packed anyway. Hilton beach in front of the hotel strip is the main peak; winter storms from the west are what everyone waits for.
info.crowd: Crowded, energetic, vocal
info.localTip: Mediterranean swell dies within hours. When a storm shows on the chart, go the same day — not the next.

access.transfer: 20 min from Ben Gurion airport
access.visaNote: Check Israel's current entry requirements for your nationality

info.about: Surfing above the Arctic Circle. Unstad is a small bay in the Lofoten Islands with a right-hand point and a left, ringed by 700-metre peaks, where you can surf under the midnight sun in summer and the northern lights in winter. The water is barely above freezing and the setting is unmatched.
info.wave: Punchy right-hand point and a shorter left
info.level: Advanced — because of the conditions, not the wave
info.bestSeason: September–March for swell; summer for midnight sun
info.waterTemp: 4–12°C — 5/4 or 6/5 with hood, gloves and boots
info.crowd: Small, dedicated crew
hazards: Near-freezing water — hypothermia is the real hazard
info.localTip: This is a full 6/5 hooded operation in winter. Warm water in a thermos for after the session is standard here.

access.transfer: About 45 min from Leknes
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The heaviest wave in the world. Teahupo'o breaks over a shallow coral shelf that rises from deep water almost vertically, so the wave does not so much break as fall — a thick slab of Pacific Ocean landing on dry reef. Olympic venue, championship tour stop, and utterly unforgiving.
info.wave: A thick, square, below-sea-level left barrel
info.crowd: A very small, very experienced crew
hazards: One of the most dangerous waves on earth
Serious injuries and deaths have occurred
Remote — the hospital is in Papeete
info.localTip: Almost everyone who comes here watches from a boat at the channel. That is the correct decision.

access.transfer: About 90 min by road from Papeete to the end of the road
access.visaNote: French Polynesia — Schengen-style rules apply for many nationalities

info.about: A left-hand reef pass a kilometre out to sea off Tavarua island, breaking over shallow coral in the middle of the Pacific. Cloudbreak is long, fast and genuinely world-class at every size, from playful head-high to the 20-foot day that produced some of the most famous images in surfing.
info.crowd: Limited — access is by boat, which caps numbers
info.localTip: Restaurants, the right next door, is shorter and lighter. Cloudbreak on a big day is a professional-level wave.

access.transfer: About 20 min by road from Nadi plus a 45-min boat transfer
access.visaNote: Many nationalities get 4 months visa-free in Fiji

info.about: Nicaragua's signature wave, backed by the most reliable offshore wind on earth: Lake Nicaragua generates a thermal breeze that blows offshore on this coast around 300 days a year. Popoyo has a sand-bottom beach break and an outer reef that holds serious size.
info.wave: Punchy peaks inside; big, powerful outer reef
info.bestWind: Offshore almost every morning thanks to the lake effect
info.crowd: Moderate — the coast is still relatively undeveloped
hazards: Strong offshore wind makes paddling back harder
info.localTip: The offshore wind that makes this coast is also relentless — a slightly bigger board helps with the paddle in.

access.transfer: About 3h south-west by road from Managua
access.visaNote: Most nationalities buy a tourist card on arrival in Nicaragua

info.about: Lisbon's home break and the most consistent beach break on the Estoril line, twenty minutes from the city centre by train. The sandbanks either side of the São Julião da Barra fort pick up almost any Atlantic swell, and the wave is forgiving enough to learn on and punchy enough to be worth the trip when it is bigger.
info.crowd: Very busy, it is Lisbon's beach
info.localTip: The train from Cais do Sodré drops you a five-minute walk from the sand, which makes it the easiest surf in Europe to reach without a car.

access.transfer: About 25 min west of Lisbon by train or car
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A wild, exposed beach at the edge of the Sintra-Cascais natural park, with dunes behind it and the Serra da Sintra rising to the north. Guincho takes more swell than anywhere else near Lisbon and is famous for the nortada, the summer north wind that made it a windsurfing and kitesurfing capital and that ruins the surf most afternoons.
info.crowd: Moderate; the wind thins the crowd
info.localTip: Surf it at dawn. By lunchtime the nortada is usually up and the sailors have it.

access.transfer: About 40 min west of Lisbon via Cascais
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A long beach below dramatic cliffs on the Sintra coast, with fossil dinosaur footprints in the rock at the north end. Praia Grande is consistent, holds size better than most beach breaks nearby and has hosted European bodyboarding events for years.
info.wave: Consistent, punchy peaks that hold size
info.crowd: Busy in summer, quiet in winter
info.localTip: The north end takes the swell first; the south end is calmer when it is big.

access.transfer: About 45 min from Lisbon via Sintra
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: A horseshoe bay on the Costa Vicentina, inside the south-west Alentejo natural park, with a fishing harbour under the cliff and a right-hand point at the north end. The headland shelters it from the north wind that blows out the rest of the west coast, which is why it works when nowhere else does.
info.wave: Long right off the point; softer peaks in the bay
info.level: Beginner in the bay, intermediate on the point
info.bestWind: N–NE offshore, and the cliff blocks the nortada
info.crowd: Busy in summer with surf schools
hazards: Strong current when it is big
Steep cliff road down to the beach
info.localTip: When the nortada is howling everywhere else on the west coast, Arrifana is the sheltered option worth the drive.

access.transfer: About 90 min north-west of Faro
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: Four and a half kilometres of beach between Biarritz and the mouth of the Adour, cut into a dozen named breaks by groynes. Les Cavaliers is the one that matters: a heavy, fast peak beside the northern jetty that has hosted European contests for decades, while Chambre d'Amour and the Sables d'Or at the southern end are gentler. The groynes hold the sand, which makes it more reliable than most French beach breaks.
info.wave: Punchy peaks; Les Cavaliers is fast and heavy
info.crowd: Busy in summer, spread over a dozen beaches
info.localTip: Walk the promenade and pick your groyne. Each bay holds a different bank, and the one that is closing out at Cavaliers is often perfect two beaches south.

access.transfer: 10 min north of Biarritz airport
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements

info.about: The longest beach in the French Basque country, three kilometres of sand on the Spanish border with the twin rocks of Les Jumeaux offshore. Cap du Figuier shelters the bay, so the waves arrive softened — which makes Hendaye the region's learn-to-surf beach, and the place everyone goes when the rest of the coast is too big to paddle out.
info.bestSwell: NW Atlantic swell, softened by the headland
info.crowd: Busy with schools in summer
hazards: Rip beside the rocks at the west end
Estuary current at the Spanish end
info.localTip: When Hossegor and Anglet are closing out, this is the bay that is still rideable.

access.transfer: About 35 min south of Biarritz; 25 min from San Sebastián
access.visaNote: Schengen area — check your entry requirements
